341.quote_or_event: “As long as I walked along, carrying the load, I continued to pay the fine. But I threw away that bundle, when I met the Perfect Guru; O Nanak, then I became fearless.”
341.explanation: Guru Arjan describes attachment to Maya as a bundle carried on the head: as long as it is carried, its penalty is paid, and once it is set down, fear and burden go with it.
341.tie_back: The Kural says that from whatever one has let go, one suffers no more pain; Guru Arjan says the same of the bundle he threw down, whose fine he no longer pays.
341.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 214, Raag Gauree (Gauree Maalaa), Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
341._accuracy_note: A strong fit on release ending the pain tied to what is released; in Gurbani the release comes through meeting the Guru, not through ascetic withdrawal.

342.quote_or_event: “Kabeer, that which you have to do tomorrow - do it today instead; and that which you have to do now - do it immediately!”
342.explanation: In his saloks Bhagat Kabir urges that the turn to God must not be postponed, because the time to act is now.
342.tie_back: The Kural asks for renunciation while one still has things to renounce, not after they have slipped away; Kabir likewise insists that the spiritual turn be made today, not tomorrow.
342.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1371, Salok Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
342._accuracy_note: The shared point is urgency and timing only; Kabir is urging remembrance of God, not the giving up of possessions, and the verse is a Bhagat's saying in the Granth, not a Guru's.

343.quote_or_event: “They conquer the five thieves, and enshrine the True Lord in the heart.”
343.explanation: Guru Nanak describes the way of life that leads to God as overcoming the five thieves (kaam, krodh, lobh, moh, ahankar) and keeping the True One in the heart.
343.tie_back: The Kural asks that the five senses be subdued and everything they crave be given up together; Guru Nanak asks for the five inner thieves to be conquered and the heart given to God instead.
343.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 223, Raag Gauree, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
343._accuracy_note: A strong thematic fit on mastering five inner forces, but Gurbani's five are passions rather than the five senses, and the Sikh remedy is enshrining God rather than withdrawing from sense objects.

344.quote_or_event: “As the lotus flower floats unaffected in the water, so does he remain detached in his own household.”
344.explanation: Guru Amar Das gives the classic Sikh image of detachment: the lotus lives in water without being wetted, and the Gurmukh lives in the family home without being bound by it.
344.tie_back: The Kural makes owning nothing the very nature of austerity; Sikh teaching answers that detachment lies in the mind, so one may keep a household and possessions and still be free of them.
344.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 949, Raag Raamkalee (Ramkali ki Vaar), Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
344._accuracy_note: Next-best and largely a contrast: Sikhism rejects the Kural's ideal of total possessionlessness and affirms the householder path, while sharing its concern that attachment, not the object, is what binds.

345.quote_or_event: “This human body has been given to you. This is your chance to meet the Lord of the Universe.”
345.explanation: Guru Arjan treats the human body as a precious opportunity, the one chance in which a soul can meet God.
345.tie_back: The Kural calls even the body one thing too many for those who seek to end rebirth; Sikh teaching shares the goal of ending rebirth but values the body as the very means of reaching it.
345.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 12, Raag Aasaa (in the So Purakh section of Rehras), Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
345._accuracy_note: Low, a deliberate contrast: Sikhism does not regard the body as an encumbrance to be shed and explicitly honours human birth, so it agrees only on the goal of liberation.

346.quote_or_event: “As long as I claimed, ‘Mine, mine!’, I was surrounded by wickedness and corruption. But when I dedicated my mind, body and intellect to my Lord and Master, then I began to sleep in peace.”
346.explanation: Guru Arjan names possessiveness, the cry of mine, as the cause of entanglement, and says peace came only when mind, body and intellect were offered to God.
346.tie_back: The Kural promises a world beyond the gods to one who cuts off the pride of I and mine; Guru Arjan describes the same cutting off of mine as the passage from corruption into peace.
346.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 214, Raag Gauree (Gauree Maalaa), Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
346._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one on giving up the sense of mine; the Sikh reward is inner peace and union with God rather than a higher heavenly world.

347.quote_or_event: “In that pool, people have made their homes, but the water there is as hot as fire! In the swamp of emotional attachment, their feet cannot move. I have seen them drowning there.”
347.explanation: Guru Nanak pictures the world as a burning pool and emotional attachment (moh) as a swamp that holds the feet fast until people drown.
347.tie_back: The Kural says sorrows grip and never release those who grip their attachments; Guru Nanak shows the same grip from the other side, a swamp of attachment that will not let the feet go.
347.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 12, Raag Aasaa (in the So Purakh section of Rehras), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
347._accuracy_note: A strong fit on attachment as a trap that holds its captive in suffering; it lacks the Kural's mirrored wordplay but carries the same moral.

348.quote_or_event: “The fish did not notice the net in the deep and salty sea.”
348.explanation: In Siree Raag Guru Nanak uses the fish caught unawares in the fisherman's net as an image of the heedless soul trapped by Maya and death.
348.tie_back: The Kural says that those who have not wholly renounced are bewildered and netted; Guru Nanak's fish, which never saw the net, is the same bewildered captive.
348.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 55, Siree Raag, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
348._accuracy_note: Reasonable but partial: the image of the heedless being netted matches closely, but Gurbani does not set complete renunciants against everyone else; its way out is the Guru and the Name.

349.quote_or_event: “Coming and going in reincarnation is ended, O Nanak, for those whose minds are filled with the Lord.”
349.explanation: Guru Arjan teaches that the round of birth and death ends for those in whose minds God dwells.
349.tie_back: The Kural says the cycle of birth is cut the moment attachment ceases, and otherwise the round of coming and going continues; Gurbani uses the same coming and going and ties its end to a mind filled with God.
349.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 251, Raag Gauree (Bavan Akhree, salok), Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
349._accuracy_note: Reasonable but partial: both speak of ending coming and going, but the Sikh condition is God dwelling in the mind rather than the cessation of attachment as such.

350.quote_or_event: “I am joined with You, and I have broken with all others.”
350.explanation: Bhagat Ravidas tells God that by joining himself to the Lord in love he has broken his bond with everything else.
350.tie_back: The Kural resolves its chapter by prescribing one attachment, to the One without attachment, so that every other may be let go; Ravidas states exactly that exchange of one bond for all others.
350.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 659, Raag Sorath, Bhagat Ravidas (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
350._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one on clinging to God alone in order to release all other ties; the verse is a Bhagat's composition included in the Granth, not a Guru's.
